Launeddas（撒丁島三管笛）是撒丁島傳統木管氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel: The launeddas (Sardinian triple pipe) is a traditional Sardinian woodwind aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.22. It consists of three reed pipes, each sounding with a single reed cut from the pipe itself; two of them are melody pipes of different lengths with five fingerholes, and the third acts as a drone. The player uses circular breathing to blow continuously, producing a polyphonic effect: the drone pipe holds a fixed note while the two melody pipes play melody in thirds and sixths. Sardinian players use it in religious ritual and dance.

The launeddas (Sardinian triple pipe) is a traditional Sardinian woodwind aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.22. It consists of three reed pipes, each sounding with a single reed cut from the pipe itself; two of them are melody pipes of different lengths with five fingerholes, and the third acts as a drone. The player uses circular breathing to blow continuously, producing a polyphonic effect: the drone pipe holds a fixed note while the two melody pipes play melody in thirds and sixths. Sardinian players use it in religious ritual and dance (Sardinian su ballu).
Launeddas（撒丁島三管笛）由三根同體單簧管構成，一管作持續音，另兩管以三: The launeddas (Sardinian triple pipe) is built of three single-reed pipes cut whole, one pipe holding a drone while the other two play melody in thirds and sixths, which produces a polyphonic effect. The player keeps the sound continuous by circular breathing, so that the music stretches on without a break through religious ritual and dance. Its sound has been described as one of the most primitive and most resonant sounds in European music.
吹奏者持撒丁島三管笛，以循環呼吸讓三管同時發聲。其中一管作持續音，另兩管為五孔旋: The player holds the Sardinian triple pipe and uses circular breathing so that all three pipes sound at once. One pipe holds the drone while the other two, melody pipes with five fingerholes, play melody in thirds and sixths. For a start, practise circular breathing and a steady drone, then get used to the changes in a small number of melodic phrases, and add the two-pipe melody gradually.

撒丁島三管笛實際用於撒丁島的宗教儀式與舞蹈場合，舞蹈在撒丁語中稱 su ball: The Sardinian triple pipe is actually used in religious ritual and dance in Sardinia, the dance being called su ballu in Sardinian. Its scoring is three pipes: one sounds a drone and the other two play melody in thirds and sixths, while circular breathing keeps the phrases continuous. Players who can be heard include Efisio Melis, Antonio Lara, Dionigi Burranca and Luigi Lai; Lara's style also passed to pupils such as Aureliu Porcu.
撒丁島三管笛由三支簧管組成，其中兩支為五孔旋律管，一支為持續音管；每支管皆以同體: The Sardinian triple pipe consists of three reed pipes, two of them melody pipes with five fingerholes and one a drone pipe; each pipe sounds by means of a single reed cut from the pipe itself. The source describes it only as a woodwind aerophone and does not state the materials of the pipe body, the reed or any other part.
撒丁島三管笛的前身見於北非與中東。西元前2700年，埃及蘆笛稱memet；舊王國: The predecessor of the Sardinian triple pipe is found in North Africa and the Middle East. In 2700 BC the Egyptian cane flute was called memet; it appears in the Old Kingdom (2778–2723 BC) in seven tombs at Saqqara, six tombs at Giza and the reliefs of Queen Khentkaus's pyramid. The Sardinian triple pipe itself goes back at least to the 8th century BC, as bronze figurines of the Nuragic period excavated at Ittiri show. The 1930s were its golden age, with Efisio Melis and Antonio Lara the most famous, each with his pupils, such as Antonio Lara's Aureliu Porcu.
